K6131 Horseshoe abscess

Surgery for abscess drainage or fistula repair (e.g., seton placement) would also indicate severe flare activity. The need for urgent/emergent surgery (such as for perforation or toxic megacolon in UC) is a clear sign of a fulminant flare.

Outpatient Visits with IBD Diagnosis Codes: Flare activity often leads to frequent or urgent physician visits. In Alberta’s claims, this may appear as ICD-9 codes 555.x (regional enteritis, Crohn’s) or 556.x (ulcerative colitis), or their ICD-10 equivalents K50/K51 in newer systems. For instance, a GI clinic visit claim coded as 555.0 (Crohn’s of small intestine) or 556.9 (UC, unspecified) suggests the visit addressed an IBD flare or related issue.
Frequency/Intensity of Visits: Repeated claims for IBD within a short period (e.g. multiple visits in a week or month) or prolonged consultations can be a marker of a flare requiring close monitoring. While a single code on a claim confirms an IBD encounter, clusters of visits (e.g. frequent GI consults, phone follow-ups) for symptoms like pain or diarrhea often coincide with flare periods. (E.g., multiple claims with IBD codes over consecutive weeks likely indicate ongoing flare management.)
IBD-specific Procedures in Ambulatory Care: Some procedures related to flares are captured in claims or ambulatory data – for example, an outpatient colonoscopy to evaluate active disease (often within NACRS, see below) or therapeutic interventions like iron infusions for anemia or IV biologic infusions administered in clinic. If these are billed through physician claims (with procedure codes or special visit codes), they further underline active disease (e.g., a claim for colonoscopy with biopsy in an IBD patient suggests assessment of flare severity).

Emergency Department (ED) Visits for IBD or Symptoms: Flares often lead patients to seek acute care. NACRS ED records with IBD diagnostic codes indicate an acute flare presentation. Examples: an ED visit coded K50.x or K51.x as the diagnosis (Crohn’s or UC), or other acute GI codes like K52.9 (colitis, unspecified) when IBD is suspected. Even symptom codes can reflect flares: abdominal pain (R10.x), diarrhea (R19.7), rectal bleeding (K62.5 or as symptom), gastrointestinal bleeding unspecified (K92.2), or dehydration (E86) from severe diarrhea are common in IBD flares. For instance, an ED visit for severe abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea that is coded as ulcerative colitis is a likely flare event.
Ambulatory Care Clinics/Day Surgery: Many IBD-related procedures and treatments occur as ambulatory visits captured by NACRS. A key example is outpatient colonoscopy during a flare to assess disease activity or complications – this might be coded with a CCI procedure code (e.g., diagnostic colonoscopy 2.NM.70 or colonoscopy with biopsy 2.NM.71). The presence of such a procedure in an IBD patient’s timeline indicates active evaluation or management of disease (often prompted by symptoms).
Infusions or Injections Visits: If biologic therapies (like infliximab) are administered in hospital outpatient infusion clinics, these visits appear in NACRS. For instance, a record of an infliximab infusion appointment (which might be coded under a therapy administration code, e.g., CCI 1.ZZ.35 for immunomodulatory infusion) suggests treatment for moderate-to-severe IBD (often corresponding to a recent or ongoing flare). Similarly, frequent IV steroid injections or rehydration IV therapy visits would align with flare management.
Urgent Ambulatory Interventions: Other NACRS events may include perianal abscess drainages, paracentesis for IBD-related ascites, or blood transfusions for severe IBD-related anemia. While these might be less common, their occurrence (coded with appropriate procedure codes) would be strong evidence of a significant flare or complication (e.g., transfusion for acute GI bleeding in ulcerative colitis).
Pharmaceutical Information Network (PIN) – Prescriptions
Corticosteroid Therapies (Systemic or Local): The initiation or dose escalation of corticosteroids is a hallmark of IBD flares. A new prescription for oral or intravenous  prednisone (typically high-dose, e.g. 40 mg daily taper) strongly indicates an active flare requiring suppression of inflammation. Likewise, budesonide prescriptions (e.g. Budesonide MMX for Crohn’s ileocolitis) or injectable/IV steroids (if recorded outside hospital) signal acute flare management. Even rectal steroids (hydrocortisone or budesonide enemas/foams) prescribed for ulcerative proctitis flares would fall in this category. (Prednisone is generally only used to settle active disease and not for maintenance, so its use is a direct flare indicator. For example, a pharmacy fill for prednisone 50mg implies a flare treatment.)
5-ASA and Related Anti-Inflammatories: An increase in 5-ASA therapy or addition of rectal 5-ASA can indicate a flare, especially in ulcerative colitis. For instance, a new or increased-dose prescription of mesalamine (5-ASA), or adding mesalamine enemas/suppositories for someone previously stable on oral therapy, suggests an active UC flare in the distal colon. (While 5-ASAs like mesalamine are maintenance drugs, intensifying therapy – e.g., going from oral to combined oral+rectal – is often done during flares.)
IMPORTANT: Continuing the same mesalazine dose that a patient has been on for maintenance is NOT a flare indicator. Only NEW prescriptions, dose increases, or formulation additions (e.g., adding rectal to oral therapy) suggest flare activity.
Immunomodulator and Biologic Initiation: Starting or escalating biologic therapy or immunosuppressants often corresponds to flare-ups or refractory disease. A PIN record showing a new anti-TNF agent (e.g., infliximab, adalimumab, golimumab, certolizumab initiation) or other biologics (vedolizumab, ustekinumab, risankizumab, mirikizumab, guselkumab etc.) indicates a moderate-to-severe flare or inadequate control on previous therapy. Similarly, starting an immunosuppressant like azathioprine, 6-mercaptopurine, or methotrexate (often used as steroid-sparing agents) may follow a flare or be part of escalation due to active disease. (Note: Continuing long-term biologic prescriptions may not always mean a current flare – but recent initiation of a biologic is a marker of recently active disease.)
Rescue and Adjunct Medications: Other medications given during flares include antibiotics (such as metronidazole or ciprofloxacin for Crohn’s disease complications like abscesses or perianal fistulas) and pain or anti-diarrheal meds. These medications may also appear in response to non-IBD medical events, so these drugs paired with IBD-related diagnoses may be treated as a stronger indicator. A prescription for metronidazole together with IBD diagnoses can mean a flare with bacterial overgrowth or fistulizing disease. Likewise, short-term use of narcotic analgesics or antidiarrheals (like loperamide or cholestyramine) may increase during flares (though these are supportive rather than specific to IBD). The most specific markers remain steroids and biologics – e.g., prednisone or infliximab usage are well-established proxies for active disease. (In one cohort, use of prednisone or infliximab was found to serve as a reliable marker of active IBD – they are typically initiated only when a patient is “truly symptomatic with active disease”.)
Dose/Frequency Changes: Pay attention to changes like a shortened biologic dosing interval (e.g., increasing infliximab frequency to q4 weeks from q8) or high refill frequency of steroids – these patterns in PIN data can reflect attempting to control a difficult flare. Also, multiple new drug starts in the same week (e.g., prednisone + an antibiotic + a biologic) would strongly imply a significant flare event.
Laboratory Results – Inflammatory Markers and Related Labs
Elevated C-Reactive Protein (CRP): CRP is a key lab marker for IBD activity. A high CRP level (above normal range, e.g. >5–10 mg/L) indicates active inflammation; conversely, a CRP < 10 mg/L is often seen in remission. CRP rises quickly in flares – values can climb into dozens of mg/L in moderate flares, and >50–100 mg/L in severe cases. For example, a CRP of 30 or 50 mg/L during a given week strongly suggests an active IBD flare (barring other infections). Note: CRP is more sensitive in Crohn’s than in UC and can occasionally be normal even in active disease, but generally CRP > 10 (or certainly > 20) is a red flag for inflammation.
Elevated Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR): An ESR above normal (e.g., >20–30 mm/hr) is another sign of inflammation. ESR rises more slowly but remains a classic marker of chronic inflammatory activity. In the context of weekly data, a jump in ESR (especially into the 30+ mm/hr range) correlates with an ongoing flare or inflammatory process. Both CRP and ESR are often monitored together; persistent elevation of either is significant.
Fecal Calprotectin: Although primarily a stool test, fecal calprotectin is a highly specific indicator of intestinal inflammation. High fecal calprotectin levels (e.g., >250 µg/g, or any result flagged as above normal) are strongly predictive of mucosal disease activity. In fact, calprotectin has >90% positive predictive value for active IBD mucosal inflammation. If available in lab data, a spike in calprotectin (or a result labeled “positive” or elevated) is a direct marker of an IBD flare in either UC or Crohn’s.
Complete Blood Count (CBC) Changes: Active flares often cause leukocytosis (high white blood cell count) and thrombocytosis (high platelet count) as part of systemic inflammation. For example, a WBC count > 11 x10^9/Lor neutrophil count elevated in the absence of infection suggests active inflammation. Platelet count is an important clue: patients with active IBD frequently have elevated platelets (sometimes >450 x10^9/L). A high platelet count can both reflect and exacerbate inflammation, and studies show platelet counts are significantly higher during IBD flares than in remission. In summary, rising WBC or platelet trends in weekly labs point toward an active flare state (e.g., platelet count jumping from 300→500 x10^9/L with symptoms).
Anemia (Low Hemoglobin): A drop in hemoglobin can indicate a flare, due to chronic blood loss or inflammation-induced anemia. For instance, a hemoglobin <120 g/L (especially if falling from a higher baseline) is common in moderate-severe flares. Iron-deficiency anemia (low ferritin, low MCV) may develop over longer term, but acutely, a significant Hb drop or need for transfusion signals active disease bleeding. Low hemoglobin is considered a marker of disease activity over time. If weekly labs show a new anemia or worsening anemia (and no other cause like menstruation or other bleeding), an IBD flare with GI blood loss is suspect.
Low Albumin: Hypoalbuminemia (serum albumin below ~35 g/L) often accompanies severe IBD flares, reflecting both malnutrition and protein-losing enteropathy from mucosal inflammation. A falling albumin during a flare week (say from 38 → 30 g/L) is a bad prognostic sign, commonly seen in hospitalized flares or fulminant colitis. It indicates significant inflammation and bowel protein loss. Thus, new or worsening hypoalbuminemia in labs is another clue to an ongoing flare (especially in UC or extensive Crohn’s).

Some clinicians track fecal lactoferrin similar to calprotectin (if available). Additionally, negative stool cultures/C. difficile tests in the context of diarrhea can indirectly support that an IBD flare (not infection) is causing the symptoms – for example, an episode of diarrhea where cultures are negative might prompt the interpretation that it’s an IBD exacerbation. (However, stool test results would be used cautiously and in combination with the above markers.)

Strictures can be chronic but an acutely inflamed stricture causing obstruction on imaging indicates an active phase. If a report mentions “new fistula” or “phlegmon” or “worsening stricture with active inflammation”, those are signs of flare-driven complications.

Key phrases would include “severe mucosal ulceration,” “friability,” “spontaneous bleeding,” “pseudopolyps,” or “exudates” – all indicating active flare in IBD. For instance, an outpatient colonoscopy report might say “active moderate ulcerative colitis with ulcerations in the transverse colon.” If such text is part of the data (e.g., in clinical notes or imaging if a fluoroscopy is done), it should be flagged as evidence of a flare. (In the context of data sources listed, colonoscopy results might be in NACRS or separate clinical documents rather than radiology, but any reference to these terms is relevant.)
Imaging notations of Response: In patients under treatment, follow-up imaging might comment on improvement or worsening. A phrase like “resolved colitis” or “decreased wall thickening compared to prior” would conversely indicate a flare has subsided. While these denote absence of flare, they help interpret the timeline (e.g., last week CT showed active colitis, this week’s CT says resolved – implying the flare was controlled in between). For building the timeline, focus on the positive findings above that denote active disease.
